items.title: Inventory publicly indexed application assets and documents
items.objective: Build a bounded inventory of in-scope hosts, routes, file types, and public documents already exposed through search indexes.
prerequisites: Written scope containing approved domains and brands
A search service used within its terms and engagement constraints
steps: Query exact in-scope domains before using brand terms
Group results by hostname, route, and document type
Record cached snippets without opening out-of-scope hosts
Ask the owner to classify uncertain assets before active testing

examples.note: Example passive query: site:example.com; treat every result as an unconfirmed lead until ownership is established.

items.manipulate: Search operators limited to approved domains, file types, and owner-approved brand names
items.secure_behavior: Search results expose only intentionally public content and current in-scope entry points.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Results reveal a sensitive document, secret-bearing snippet, obsolete application, or privileged route with a demonstrable security consequence.
items.validation: Open only confirmed in-scope results, verify the current origin response, and distinguish stale index snippets from live exposure.
false_positives: Search indexes can retain stale snippets after content removal
Brand terms can identify unrelated third-party or similarly named organizations
items.impact: Public indexing can reveal attack-surface leads; report risk only when a live sensitive exposure or unsafe asset is confirmed.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Conduct Search Engine Discovery Reconnaissance for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Remove sensitive public content at its source, require authorization where appropriate, return correct cache directives, and request de-indexing only after the exposure is fixed.

items.title: Derive candidate hostnames from certificate transparency records
items.objective: Identify historical and current hostname candidates disclosed in public certificate transparency logs without assuming they remain owned or reachable.
steps: Query exact approved domain suffixes
Normalize wildcard and case variants
Separate current certificates from expired historical entries
Resolve candidates passively and submit uncertain ownership for confirmation

examples.note: A certificate name such as api.example.com is a candidate, not proof that the host exists or is in scope.

items.manipulate: Certificate log queries for exact approved DNS suffixes
items.secure_behavior: Certificate names align with the current asset inventory or point to safely retired names with no controllable dependency.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A certificate-derived name leads to an untracked live service or a reclaimable external dependency after separate confirmation.
items.validation: Correlate log entries with current DNS, certificate dates, and owner inventory; do not probe an unresolved or third-party address without approval.
false_positives: Expired certificates preserve names for retired systems
Wildcard certificates do not prove every possible subdomain exists
items.impact: Certificate logs can expand asset discovery; impact depends on a separately verified exposed or reclaimable service.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Conduct Search Engine Discovery Reconnaissance for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Maintain a certificate and hostname inventory, retire DNS and external dependencies with services, and avoid unnecessary names in publicly trusted certificates.

items.title: Map authoritative DNS records and external service dependencies
items.objective: Document in-scope DNS records, delegation, aliases, mail and service records, and third-party targets that define the reachable application boundary.
steps: Query authoritative NS, A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, and relevant SRV records
Follow aliases without crossing into active testing of third parties
Record TTLs and provider ownership
Flag dangling-looking targets for controlled provider-specific validation

examples.note: A CNAME to an unresolvable provider name is a lead only; claimability must be proven safely with the owner and provider rules.

items.manipulate: DNS query type and exact approved name
items.secure_behavior: Records point to owned, expected, and actively managed destinations; retired services have no residual aliases.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A record delegates trust to an unintended or demonstrably reclaimable destination, or exposes an untracked in-scope service.
items.validation: Confirm answers from authoritative servers and verify ownership/claimability without registering or taking control of any resource.
false_positives: Split-horizon DNS can intentionally differ by resolver location
A provider target may be reserved to the customer even when it does not resolve publicly
items.impact: Unsafe DNS dependencies can expose shadow services or enable domain-level trust abuse if a target is genuinely reclaimable.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Enumerate Applications on Webserver

items.remediation: Remove stale records atomically with service retirement, continuously inventory aliases, and verify external resource ownership before deployment.
items.safety: Do not register, claim, or modify a suspected dangling service. Validate ownership with the application owner and provider documentation.
do_not_report: Do not report the existence of DNS records, CDN aliases, or mail records as findings; report only misconfigurations with security impact such as dangling references, exposed management services, or mail-security failures enabling impersonation.

items.title: Correlate resolved addresses with approved hosting boundaries
items.objective: Determine which resolved addresses, networks, and delivery providers belong to the approved application path without expanding scope by IP association alone.
prerequisites: Owner guidance on shared hosting, CDN, and cloud boundaries
steps: Resolve approved hostnames from an agreed vantage point
Record address family, ASN, and reverse name as contextual evidence
Identify CDN or shared-hosting indicators
Request owner confirmation before treating adjacent names or addresses as targets

examples.note: Multiple customers can share one CDN address; co-residence never makes neighboring hosts in scope.

items.manipulate: Passive DNS and registry lookups for addresses already returned by approved names
items.secure_behavior: The resolved delivery path matches documented providers and does not reveal an unexpected directly reachable origin.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A confirmed in-scope address exposes an unintended origin or management service after separate, authorized verification.
items.validation: Correlate DNS, certificate, response, and owner evidence; avoid reverse-IP lists as proof of ownership.
false_positives: CDN and shared-hosting addresses serve unrelated tenants
Reverse DNS names commonly identify provider infrastructure rather than the application owner
items.impact: Accurate hosting boundaries prevent missed origins and, equally, prevent unauthorized testing of unrelated tenants.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Application Architecture

items.remediation: Document delivery providers and origin exposure, restrict origins to trusted edges, and keep scope records aligned with DNS changes.

items.title: Identify reachable web services on owner-approved ports
items.objective: Discover HTTP-speaking services on explicitly approved hosts and ports using conservative connection limits.
prerequisites: An owner-approved host and port range
steps: Start with ports declared by the owner and URL hints
Open a bounded TCP connection and send a harmless HTTP request
Record protocol, redirect, certificate, and response title
Stop on instability and classify each service before deeper testing

examples.request:
HEAD / HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Connection: close

items.manipulate: Destination port, HTTP version, and TLS negotiation within the approved list
items.secure_behavior: Only expected, supported services are reachable and each redirects or responds according to its documented purpose.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unexpected in-scope service exposes a sensitive interface or obsolete component after targeted confirmation.
items.validation: Repeat with the correct Host value and protocol; distinguish a generic shared listener from an application-specific service.
false_positives: A load balancer can return the same default response on many ports
A TCP listener may not belong to the scoped application despite sharing an address
items.impact: Unexpected services enlarge the attack surface; severity depends on the functionality and weakness confirmed there.
tools: nmap with an approved port list

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Enumerate Applications on Webserver

items.remediation: Remove unnecessary listeners, restrict management services by network and identity, and maintain an owner-reviewed service inventory.
items.safety: Use the owner-approved port list, low concurrency, and connection timeouts. Do not run broad Internet-scale or denial-of-service service detection.

items.title: Fingerprint the web server from multiple response characteristics
items.objective: Form a confidence-rated web-server hypothesis from headers, error behavior, protocol details, and default content rather than one banner.
prerequisites: Permission for one harmless missing-path request
steps: Record normal response headers and protocol behavior
Request a unique missing path
Compare error layout, header ordering, cookie style, and redirect syntax
Document supporting and contradictory signals
items.manipulate: A unique non-existent path and harmless Accept value
items.secure_behavior: Responses minimize precise product detail and no identified component is shown to be exploitable.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A precise obsolete server version is consistently exposed and tied to a reachable, applicable weakness.
items.validation: Require at least two independent signals and verify claimed versions against owner or package evidence before reporting risk.
false_positives: Proxies rewrite Server headers and error pages
Custom error templates can imitate another server
items.impact: Fingerprinting guides testing but is informational unless a supported exploit path or sensitive disclosure is separately proven.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Fingerprint Web Server

items.remediation: Suppress unnecessary version details, replace default error pages, and keep every server and proxy layer supported and patched.

items.title: Inventory TLS certificate names and endpoint relationships
items.objective: Use certificates presented by approved HTTPS endpoints to identify related names and delivery boundaries without treating SAN membership as scope authorization.
steps: Capture the leaf and issuing chain from each approved endpoint
Record SAN names, issuer, validity, and wildcard coverage
Deduplicate names and compare with the owner inventory
Submit new names for scope confirmation before requests

examples.note: A SAN entry is an ownership clue, not permission to connect to that hostname.

items.manipulate: TLS SNI using already approved hostnames
items.secure_behavior: Certificates cover expected services and do not reveal unmanaged application endpoints.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A certificate-derived name leads to a confirmed unmanaged or sensitive in-scope service after owner approval.
items.validation: Confirm certificate observations from the correct SNI endpoint and obtain explicit scope for every newly discovered name.
false_positives: Multi-tenant certificates can contain names owned by other customers
Historical or wildcard names do not prove a live service
items.impact: Certificate relationships improve inventory completeness; direct security impact requires a separately confirmed exposed asset.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Application Architecture

items.remediation: Use managed certificate inventories, remove obsolete names during renewal, and monitor issuance for unexpected approved-domain certificates.

items.title: Review robots directives without treating hidden paths as authorization
items.objective: Identify paths disclosed through robots.txt and determine whether any lead exposes sensitive functionality independently of crawler directives.
steps: Request /robots.txt once
Parse User-agent, Allow, Disallow, and Sitemap values
Resolve only same-origin paths
Test access controls on sensitive-looking paths separately and conservatively

examples.response:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain

User-agent: *
Disallow: /internal-preview/

items.manipulate: The standard robots.txt path and same-origin paths it explicitly lists
items.secure_behavior: Directives contain no unnecessary sensitive route names, and listed paths enforce their own authentication and authorization.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A listed path exposes sensitive data or functionality without required access control; the directive itself is only discovery evidence.
items.validation: Request the listed path in the correct auth context and prove the underlying exposure rather than reporting Disallow alone.
false_positives: Disallow is a crawler preference, not an access-control mechanism
Paths may be obsolete or intentionally public
items.impact: Robots directives can disclose useful route names, but impact derives from the confirmed weakness at a listed path.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webserver Metafiles for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Avoid advertising sensitive implementation paths and enforce authentication and authorization independently of crawler directives.

items.title: Enumerate sitemap entries and reconcile them with the route inventory
items.objective: Use declared sitemaps to identify public routes, locales, content families, and obsolete entries while preserving same-origin scope.
steps: Discover Sitemap directives and request standard sitemap locations
Parse nested indexes with a strict document and URL limit
Normalize same-origin URLs and group route patterns
Classify redirects, missing pages, and sensitive-looking routes
items.manipulate: Standard sitemap paths and same-origin URLs declared by them
items.secure_behavior: Sitemaps list intended public content and do not expose unauthorized resources or stale sensitive routes.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A sitemap entry leads to a live sensitive resource that lacks required access control or reveals confidential content.
items.validation: Verify current response and intended audience; a stale URL or public route name alone is not a finding.
false_positives: Sitemaps often retain URLs that now redirect or return 404
Localized duplicates can appear to be separate applications
items.impact: Sitemaps improve route coverage; impact depends on a confirmed exposure behind an entry.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webserver Metafiles for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Generate sitemaps from intended public routes, remove retired entries, and enforce resource authorization regardless of listing.

items.title: Inspect standardized well-known resources for security and identity metadata
items.objective: Identify intentionally published security contacts, identity metadata, and protocol configuration under standardized well-known paths.
prerequisites: A protocol-informed list of relevant well-known names
steps: Request /.well-known/security.txt
Request only well-known resources relevant to observed identity or application protocols
Record redirects and declared endpoints
Classify metadata as intended publication, stale configuration, or a lead requiring protocol-specific testing
items.manipulate: A short allowlist of standardized /.well-known/ resource names
items.secure_behavior: Published metadata is current, minimally scoped, and points only to intended endpoints.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Stale or unsafe metadata redirects trust to an unintended endpoint or exposes a demonstrable sensitive configuration.
items.validation: Verify the governing standard and active consumer behavior; metadata presence or absence alone is not a vulnerability.
false_positives: Many well-known resources are intentionally public
An unused protocol document may have no security effect
items.impact: Metadata can reveal protocol surfaces or create trust redirection when actively consumed and misconfigured.
evidence: Consumer behavior if risk is claimed

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webserver Metafiles for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Publish only required well-known metadata, keep endpoints and contacts current, and remove configuration for retired protocols.

items.title: Enumerate distinct applications behind approved hostnames and base paths
items.objective: Separate applications, tenant portals, management surfaces, and route roots that share an approved hostname or delivery address.
steps: Compare titles, cookies, headers, CSP, and redirect behavior across known base paths
Group routes that share an authentication and deployment boundary
Identify management or tenant-specific roots from links and redirects
Record each application as a separate inventory object

examples.note: Distinct cookies and login redirects under /portal and /admin can indicate separate applications even on one origin.

items.manipulate: Known base paths and owner-approved virtual host values
items.secure_behavior: Every reachable application is inventoried, supported, and protected according to its intended audience.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An untracked application exposes sensitive functionality or an obsolete component after separate testing.
items.validation: Use multiple boundary signals and owner confirmation; visual differences alone may reflect one application's theme or route.
false_positives: One application can use different frontends for routes or locales
A default virtual-host page may not represent a separate deployed application
items.impact: Accurate application boundaries prevent coverage gaps; finding severity depends on a weakness confirmed in an untracked application.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Enumerate Applications on Webserver

items.remediation: Maintain a route-to-application inventory, remove default sites, and apply consistent ownership and lifecycle controls to every deployed application.

items.title: Compare approved virtual hosts for routing and default-site behavior
items.objective: Determine how the front end routes approved Host values and whether an unintended default site exposes application or management content.
prerequisites: A shared front-end address confirmed by the owner
steps: Capture a baseline for each approved hostname
Send a request with an owner-approved alternate Host to the same address
Use one reserved invalid Host as a default-site control
Compare certificate, status, redirects, cookies, and body identity

examples.request:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: invalid.example.test
Connection: close

items.manipulate: The Host field using approved names and one reserved invalid control
items.secure_behavior: Unknown hosts are rejected and each approved host routes only to its intended application.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unrecognized or lower-trust host reaches a sensitive default application or bypasses a host-specific control.
items.validation: Pin the connection only where authorized and reproduce with controls; redirects to a canonical public host are usually benign.
false_positives: A canonical redirect for every unknown host can be intentional
CDN edge behavior may differ from the origin while still enforcing application controls
items.impact: Unsafe virtual-host routing can expose hidden applications or undermine host-based security assumptions.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Enumerate Applications on Webserver

items.remediation: Configure an explicit deny-by-default virtual host, validate accepted hosts, and keep management applications on separately controlled origins.
items.safety: Use only owner-approved connection targets and Host values plus a reserved invalid control; do not brute-force third-party virtual hosts.

items.title: Review HTML comments, metadata, and disabled interface fragments
items.objective: Identify comments, metadata, hidden fields, and disabled markup that disclose sensitive implementation details or reachable functions.
steps: Inspect raw HTML rather than only the rendered DOM
Search comments, meta elements, hidden inputs, templates, and disabled controls
Extract route or identifier leads without assuming they are secret
Verify any sensitive value or reachable function separately

examples.response: <!-- Internal deployment note: remove /legacy-admin before release -->
examples.note: A comment is a lead; report only live sensitive exposure or secret material.

items.manipulate: Normal page navigation and view-source inspection
items.secure_behavior: Markup contains no credentials, secrets, confidential comments, or reliance on hidden controls for authorization.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Source includes a valid secret or leads to a live unauthorized sensitive function after confirmation.
items.validation: Test whether values are current and whether referenced routes enforce server-side controls; redact secrets immediately.
false_positives: Placeholder keys can resemble production secrets
Disabled controls can represent intentionally inaccessible or unfinished UI with correct server authorization
items.impact: Disclosed internals can accelerate attacks; valid secrets or unauthorized functions can have direct confidentiality or access impact.
evidence: Secret validity or route authorization confirmation

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webpage Content for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Remove sensitive build comments and secrets, keep server authorization independent of UI visibility, and scan release artifacts for confidential markers.

items.title: Extract routes and service origins from first-party JavaScript
items.objective: Expand the route inventory from first-party script literals, request constructors, routers, and environment configuration.
prerequisites: First-party scripts loaded by an approved page
A bounded parser that does not execute downloaded code
steps: Inventory same-origin and owner-confirmed first-party script assets
Search statically for URL literals, route declarations, request calls, and service origins
Normalize and deduplicate candidates
Confirm scope before requesting newly identified origins or routes

examples.note: Static text can be dead code or a build-time fallback.

items.manipulate: Downloaded first-party text processed offline; no script execution
items.secure_behavior: Client artifacts expose only intended public routing knowledge and no secret-bearing configuration.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An artifact contains a valid secret or reveals a live sensitive endpoint that lacks required protection after separate confirmation.
items.validation: Trace candidates to live application behavior or owner documentation; distinguish source text, dead code, and third-party libraries.
false_positives: Bundled dead code can reference retired endpoints
Library examples and source comments can look like application routes
items.impact: Script analysis improves endpoint coverage; direct impact requires a valid secret or confirmed weakness at a discovered endpoint.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webpage Content for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Exclude secrets and private environment configuration from client builds, remove dead endpoints, and treat every client-visible route as public knowledge.

items.title: Locate and classify JavaScript source maps
items.objective: Determine whether deployed scripts reference source maps and whether those maps disclose non-public source, paths, or configuration.
prerequisites: First-party JavaScript assets from approved pages
steps: Inspect SourceMap and sourceMappingURL references
Request only maps explicitly referenced by first-party assets
Record sources, embedded content, paths, and names
Search locally for secrets and sensitive routes, then validate any lead
items.manipulate: Explicit source-map URLs declared by approved first-party scripts
items.secure_behavior: Production maps are absent, access-controlled where appropriate, or contain no sensitive source/configuration beyond intended public code.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A map exposes valid secrets, confidential source, or security-relevant implementation details with demonstrated impact.
items.validation: Confirm map ownership and secret validity; readable source alone is not automatically a vulnerability for client-delivered code.
false_positives: Minified client code is already public even without a map
Paths and variable names can be non-sensitive developer metadata
items.impact: Source maps can reduce reverse-engineering effort or expose embedded secrets and internal paths.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webpage Content for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Disable production source-map publication or restrict access, strip embedded secrets, and keep client artifacts free of confidential server code.

items.title: Catalog forms, controls, and client-visible input constraints
items.objective: Inventory user-controlled fields, submission targets, methods, encodings, and client-side constraints across representative workflows.
prerequisites: Representative pages and approved test roles
steps: Record each form action, method, encoding, and submit control
List visible, hidden, disabled, and dynamically created fields
Capture browser validation attributes and JavaScript preprocessing
Map each control to its resulting request parameter

examples.request:
POST /profile HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

displayName=Tester

items.manipulate: Normal form values on designated test data
items.secure_behavior: All intended inputs are inventoried and server-side controls do not rely solely on client constraints.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A client-hidden or constrained field changes a security-sensitive server decision after separate validation.
items.validation: Correlate each UI control with the actual request and server behavior; client-only min/max or disabled state is not a finding by itself.
false_positives: Hidden fields can be harmless state or anti-CSRF values
Client constraints may be usability controls backed by correct server validation
items.impact: A complete input map enables targeted validation and authorization testing; impact comes from a confirmed server-side weakness.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Document server input contracts, enforce them server-side, and avoid placing authoritative security state in client-editable fields.

items.title: Inventory request parameters across URL, body, headers, and cookies
items.objective: Build a deduplicated parameter inventory including location, data type, examples, authentication context, and observed server use.
steps: Walk approved workflows through an intercepting proxy
Record path, query, body, header, and cookie inputs
Infer types only from repeated observations
Mark identifiers, redirect targets, URLs, filenames, and structured values for later tests

examples.request:
GET /orders?status=open&page=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Cookie: session=REDACTED

items.manipulate: Normal workflow values; active mutation belongs to the relevant later methodology item
items.secure_behavior: The inventory matches documented inputs and no unexpected client-controlled security decision is identified.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A parameter later proves to control a sensitive action without required validation or authorization; discovery alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Replay a baseline to confirm the parameter reaches the intended route, avoiding mutation during inventory collection.
false_positives: Analytics and tracing parameters may not reach application logic
Framework-generated fields can be integrity-protected or ignored
items.impact: Parameter coverage is a prerequisite for complete injection, access-control, SSRF, redirect, and file-handling testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Maintain explicit input contracts, reject unknown fields where appropriate, and keep security decisions on trusted server state.

items.title: Map route and HTTP method combinations from observed traffic
items.objective: Create a canonical route-method inventory that distinguishes read, mutation, upload, authentication, and administrative operations.
steps: Normalize concrete identifiers into route templates
Group requests by method, content type, response family, and role
Preserve distinct methods for one route
Highlight unobserved but documented operations for later confirmation

examples.note: Normalize /api/orders/10293 to /api/orders/{id} while retaining GET and PATCH as separate operations.

items.manipulate: Offline normalization of captured request metadata
items.secure_behavior: The resulting inventory is explainable by intended workflows and documented interfaces.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A route-method combination exposes an undocumented sensitive operation after separate authorization or method testing.
items.validation: Compare normalized entries with raw requests so IDs, versions, and nested resources are not accidentally merged.
false_positives: Different concrete paths can share a shape but route to distinct handlers
HEAD and OPTIONS may be generated by infrastructure rather than application features
items.impact: A reliable operation inventory prevents gaps in method, authorization, and input testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Maintain a versioned API and route inventory, remove obsolete handlers, and enforce controls for every method independently.

items.title: Trace multi-step application execution paths and state transitions
items.objective: Document valid workflow states, transitions, prerequisites, terminal outcomes, and rollback paths before testing sequence abuse.
prerequisites: Owner-defined stopping points for consequential actions
steps: Perform each workflow normally with a test record
Name each server-observable state and transition request
Record tokens, identifiers, roles, and expiry assumptions
Diagram alternate, cancellation, retry, and error paths

examples.note: Example state path: draft → reviewed → approved → fulfilled; record the exact request that advances each transition.

items.manipulate: Normal workflow navigation and reversible test records
items.secure_behavior: Observed transitions match documented business rules and preserve required identity, approval, and state prerequisites.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later test confirms a transition can be skipped, replayed, or performed by an unauthorized actor; the map itself is not a finding.
items.validation: Verify states from fresh server responses or owner-approved records rather than relying only on client labels.
false_positives: UI step numbers may not correspond to server states
Asynchronous workflows can expose temporary intermediate states by design
items.impact: Execution-path mapping enables precise workflow, race, authorization, and replay testing with less production risk.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Execution Paths Through Application

items.remediation: Document and enforce server-side state machines with explicit transition authorization, idempotency, and safe rollback behavior.
items.safety: Use disposable records, stop before payments/fulfillment or irreversible actions, and document cleanup for every traversed path.

items.title: Identify authentication, reauthentication, and step-up entry points
items.objective: Catalog every route and protocol that establishes, refreshes, elevates, or re-verifies user identity.
prerequisites: A confirmed login or identity flow
Available test roles or owner documentation
steps: Record primary login requests and redirects
Locate reauthentication and step-up prompts in sensitive workflows
Identify token issuance, refresh, logout, and device-trust endpoints
Separate local, federated, API, and alternate-channel flows

examples.note: Record both /login and an IdP redirect/callback pair when the application uses federation.

items.manipulate: Normal identity flows with designated test accounts
items.secure_behavior: All identity entry points are inventoried and apply controls appropriate to their assurance and channel.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An alternate entry point later proves weaker and can establish or elevate identity without equivalent assurance.
items.validation: Confirm each endpoint's identity effect using a test account; route names alone do not establish authentication behavior.
false_positives: A login-looking page can be a static redirector
Token endpoints may belong to a separate, out-of-scope identity provider
items.impact: Missing alternate identity paths can leave authentication, MFA, session, and recovery coverage incomplete.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Maintain one reviewed identity-flow inventory and apply equivalent assurance, logging, and lifecycle controls across every entry point.

items.title: Map registration, invitation, recovery, and account-change flows
items.objective: Document account lifecycle flows, trust transitions, tokens, communication channels, and identity attributes before targeted abuse testing.
steps: Run registration or invitation through its approved stopping point
Map verification, activation, recovery, email/phone change, and cancellation
Record token transport, expiry, account state, and identity-binding fields
Identify alternate channels and support-assisted transitions

examples.note: Use only controlled inboxes and never trigger messages to real users during lifecycle mapping.

items.manipulate: Normal lifecycle inputs for designated test identities
items.secure_behavior: Every lifecycle transition has a documented identity proof, bounded token, and consistent final account state.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later test confirms an unverified or unauthorized transition; discovery of a flow alone is not a vulnerability.
items.validation: Confirm account state through a fresh session or owner-approved record and distinguish UI completion from server activation.
false_positives: Invitation and open registration can be intentionally different assurance paths
A generic success message may intentionally conceal whether an account exists
items.impact: Lifecycle mapping enables complete enumeration, recovery, token, MFA, and account-binding tests.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Execution Paths Through Application

items.remediation: Document lifecycle assurance requirements, bind single-use expiring tokens to the intended account/action, and verify sensitive identity changes.
items.safety: Use controlled addresses and numbers, cap messages, avoid support burden, and remove disposable accounts when testing ends.

items.title: Discover API base paths, versions, and content types
items.objective: Build an evidence-based inventory of HTTP API roots, versions, media types, and consumers from observed application traffic.
steps: Filter captured requests for structured response media types and API path patterns
Group operations by origin, base path, and version
Record JSON, XML, form, multipart, and custom media types
Reconcile old and current versions with owner documentation

examples.request:
GET /api/v2/profile HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json

items.manipulate: Normal API requests generated by approved clients
items.secure_behavior: Reachable API versions and media types are inventoried, supported, and intentionally exposed.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An undocumented or retired API version exposes weaker controls or sensitive data after separate testing.
items.validation: Confirm operations from actual traffic or documentation; do not infer a complete API from a path naming convention.
false_positives: A path containing api may return static content
Multiple media types can be intentional representations of one operation
items.impact: API inventory completeness is required for authorization, input, data exposure, and version-retirement testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Maintain a consumer-aware API inventory, publish supported versions, and remove or equivalently secure deprecated operations.

items.title: Locate OpenAPI and interactive API documentation
items.objective: Find owner-intended API schemas and interactive documentation, then compare their operation inventory and exposure with deployed behavior.
prerequisites: An approved API origin or owner-confirmed documentation location
steps: Check links and standard documentation paths only on approved origins
Record schema version, servers, operations, security schemes, and examples
Determine intended audience and access control
Compare documented versions with observed traffic
items.manipulate: A short reviewed list of documentation paths such as /openapi.json and linked schema URLs
items.secure_behavior: Documentation exposure matches its intended audience, contains no secrets, and accurately represents supported operations.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A schema exposes sensitive internal-only operations, valid credentials, or reachable undocumented administrative functions with demonstrated impact.
items.validation: Confirm operation reachability and intended audience; public API documentation is not inherently a vulnerability.
false_positives: Public APIs intentionally publish complete schemas
Example tokens and hosts may be inert placeholders
items.impact: Schemas accelerate attack-surface discovery; direct impact requires sensitive content or an improperly exposed operation.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Publish schemas deliberately, remove secrets and internal-only operations, require appropriate access, and keep deployed and documented inventories synchronized.

items.title: Discover GraphQL endpoint locations and accepted transports
items.objective: Find every reachable GraphQL endpoint and record which HTTP methods, content types, persisted-query modes, and subscription channels each accepts before GraphQL-specific testing.
prerequisites: GraphQL selected or suggested during scope
Observed client traffic or owner documentation
steps: Trace application requests for GraphQL operation documents
Record endpoint, method, content type, operation name, and auth context
Identify GET, POST, persisted-query, multipart, and subscription transports actually used
Use a minimal typename query only when explicitly permitted

examples.request:
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"query":"query ScopeCheck { __typename }"}

items.manipulate: A minimal owner-approved GraphQL operation and observed transport fields
items.secure_behavior: GraphQL is exposed only at intended endpoints and each transport enters the same authentication and authorization boundary.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An alternate endpoint or transport later proves to bypass required controls; endpoint confirmation alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Require a GraphQL-shaped response or owner confirmation; a route named graphql that returns generic errors is insufficient.
false_positives: REST endpoints can use JSON fields named query
A development IDE path can exist while the GraphQL service remains correctly protected
items.impact: Transport inventory prevents gaps in GraphQL authorization, complexity, batching, upload, and subscription testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Maintain one GraphQL endpoint inventory and apply consistent authentication, authorization, parser, and resource controls to every transport.

items.title: Identify WebSocket and server-sent event channels
items.objective: Catalog persistent browser channels, handshake URLs, subprotocols, authentication transport, and message or event families.
prerequisites: A feature using live updates, chat, notifications, or streaming
steps: Observe browser network activity during real-time features
Record WebSocket handshakes and EventSource requests
Identify cookies, query tokens, subprotocols, reconnect behavior, and channel identifiers
Classify representative inbound and outbound message types without mutation

examples.request:
GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Origin: https://app.example.com

items.manipulate: Normal feature actions that establish or subscribe to a designated test channel
items.secure_behavior: Every persistent channel is inventoried and uses intended authentication, origin, subscription, and message boundaries.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An alternate channel or subscription later permits unauthorized data or action; channel existence alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Correlate the channel with a user action and test identity; distinguish first-party channels from third-party analytics or support widgets.
false_positives: Third-party widgets can open channels outside application ownership
Public event feeds may intentionally require no authentication
items.impact: Channel inventory enables complete handshake, message authorization, subscription, replay, and origin testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Document persistent channels and enforce consistent identity, origin, subscription, message-schema, and lifecycle controls.

items.title: Fingerprint server-side application frameworks with corroborating signals
items.objective: Identify likely server-side frameworks from independent cookies, headers, paths, error forms, and generated markup with an explicit confidence level.
steps: Collect framework indicators from at least two response classes
Separate generic language/runtime signals from framework-specific markers
Compare signals with official framework documentation
Record conflicting indicators and avoid assigning a version without proof

examples.note: A JSESSIONID cookie suggests a Java servlet environment but does not identify the framework or version.

items.manipulate: A harmless missing path and normal content negotiation
items.secure_behavior: Framework details are minimized and deployed versions remain supported; obscurity is not treated as the primary control.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A precisely confirmed obsolete framework exposes a reachable applicable weakness after separate validation.
items.validation: Require multiple independent signals or owner/build evidence; automated fingerprint labels alone are insufficient.
false_positives: Applications can retain legacy cookie names after migration
Reverse proxies and shared templates can add framework-like markers
items.impact: Framework confidence focuses later template, serialization, routing, and configuration tests; it is normally informational alone.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Fingerprint Web Application Framework

items.remediation: Remove unnecessary framework disclosures, standardize safe errors, track dependencies, and keep frameworks supported and patched.

items.title: Identify packaged applications and content management systems
items.objective: Determine whether an in-scope site is a known packaged application or CMS using multiple current, non-invasive markers.
prerequisites: A marker set that uses harmless public requests
steps: Inspect generator metadata, public assets, route conventions, and cookies
Request only a small set of high-confidence public markers
Compare at least two independent indicators
Record product/version confidence separately and avoid broad plugin enumeration

examples.note: A /wp-content/ asset is a WordPress-family indicator, not proof of an exact core or plugin version.

items.manipulate: A bounded list of public product marker paths
items.secure_behavior: The application exposes no unnecessary precise versions and supported components are maintained.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A confirmed obsolete product or extension has a reachable applicable weakness after controlled validation.
items.validation: Use multiple markers and owner/package evidence where possible; do not map a banner directly to a CVE.
false_positives: CDNs and migrations can preserve old product asset paths
Themes can copy marker files from another application
items.impact: Product identification directs relevant tests; direct risk requires confirmed version, reachability, and exploitability.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Fingerprint Web Application

items.remediation: Remove default/version artifacts where practical, maintain an accurate component inventory, and promptly update or retire packaged applications and extensions.
items.safety: Disable aggressive plugin/path enumeration and keep requests to a short reviewed marker list with normal rate limits.

items.title: Map reverse proxies, CDNs, gateways, and application tiers
items.objective: Develop a confidence-rated model of request hops and trust boundaries from protocol, headers, caching, errors, DNS, and owner evidence.
steps: Record DNS and TLS delivery-provider indicators
Compare headers, request IDs, caching, and errors across routes
Identify gateway-added versus origin-added behavior
Diagram browser, edge, gateway, service, identity, and data boundaries with confidence labels

examples.note: Via, trace, and CDN headers are clues; absence does not prove a direct-to-origin architecture.

items.manipulate: Normal requests to representative public and authenticated routes
items.secure_behavior: The observed path matches documented architecture and trust-bearing headers are created and consumed only at intended hops.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later test confirms a trust-boundary bypass, exposed origin, or inconsistent control between paths; the inferred diagram alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Reconcile external observations with owner diagrams or logs and preserve uncertainty where components cannot be distinguished.
false_positives: Header names can be application-generated rather than proxy-generated
Different route behavior can reflect configuration rather than separate tiers
items.impact: Architecture mapping is essential for host trust, cache, smuggling, origin, authorization, and logging tests.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Application Architecture

items.remediation: Document and minimize trust boundaries, authenticate internal hops, strip untrusted forwarding headers, and keep controls consistent across every route to origin.

items.title: Compare edge and suspected origin behavior without bypassing scope
items.objective: Determine whether an owner-confirmed origin is directly reachable and applies security controls equivalent to the intended edge path.
prerequisites: Owner confirmation of the origin address or hostname
steps: Capture a baseline through the normal public hostname
Connect to the owner-confirmed origin using correct SNI and Host
Compare authentication, routing, filtering, caching, and security headers
Stop if the origin serves unrelated tenants or unexpected content

examples.note: Never derive and probe suspected cloud addresses without owner confirmation; shared infrastructure can host unrelated customers.

items.manipulate: Connection destination while preserving approved SNI, Host, route, and harmless method
items.secure_behavior: Origins reject untrusted direct access or enforce controls equivalent to the approved edge path.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Direct access to a confirmed origin bypasses a security-relevant edge control with demonstrable impact.
items.validation: Show a paired edge/origin difference using the same request and verify the missing control is actually security-relevant.
false_positives: Diagnostic headers can differ while security decisions remain equivalent
The address can belong to shared infrastructure or a retired origin
items.impact: A direct-origin bypass can evade authentication gates, filtering, rate controls, or cache protections depending on architecture.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Application Architecture

items.remediation: Restrict origins to authenticated edge traffic, enforce critical controls at the trusted service layer, and monitor direct access attempts.
items.safety: Do not probe guessed origins. Use only an owner-confirmed destination, one harmless route, correct SNI/Host, and stop on unrelated content.

items.title: Reconcile administrative and non-production hostnames with scope
items.objective: Identify admin, development, staging, test, and preview hostname candidates and determine ownership, exposure, and lifecycle status before testing.
prerequisites: Passive hostname sources or URL hints
steps: Collect exact environment-label candidates from approved passive sources
Resolve and inspect certificates without brute-forcing names
Ask the owner to classify each live candidate
Apply active testing only after explicit inclusion and environment safety guidance

examples.note: staging.example.com is a low-confidence environment clue; the label does not prove weaker controls or permission to test.

items.manipulate: Passive records and owner-approved hostname requests
items.secure_behavior: Administrative and non-production services are intentionally exposed, access-restricted, inventoried, and free of production secrets/data.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A confirmed in-scope environment exposes sensitive access, data, or exploitable weak controls after separate validation.
items.validation: Confirm ownership, environment purpose, and data sensitivity; labels and login pages alone are not findings.
false_positives: Environment-like labels can front production services
A hostname may resolve to a generic deny page or shared edge
items.impact: Unmanaged environments can expose weaker controls or sensitive data, but impact must be demonstrated in the confirmed environment.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Enumerate Applications on Webserver

items.remediation: Inventory and access-restrict every environment, prohibit production secrets/data in lower tiers, and remove DNS when environments are retired.
items.safety: Do not actively test a discovered admin or non-production host until the owner confirms scope, data handling, and safe test limits.

items.title: Inventory third-party scripts, frames, APIs, and identity dependencies
items.objective: Document external origins that receive data, execute in the page, frame content, provide identity, or supply security-relevant application functions.
prerequisites: Owner distinction between first and third parties
steps: Extract external origins from network traffic, markup, CSP, and redirects
Classify scripts, frames, APIs, analytics, support, payment, storage, and identity services
Record data sent and browser privilege
Confirm whether each provider is in scope, dependency-only, or separately authorized

examples.note: Loading a script from a provider gives it page execution privilege but does not authorize testing the provider.

items.manipulate: Normal application workflows while observing external requests
items.secure_behavior: Every external dependency is approved, minimally privileged, data-appropriate, and governed by an owner.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A dependency relationship later enables sensitive data leakage, unsafe trust, or a confirmed integration weakness; presence alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Separate first-party aliases from third parties and verify actual transmitted fields with secrets and personal data redacted.
false_positives: A DNS alias can make a first-party service appear external
Browser extensions can inject unrelated third-party requests
items.impact: Third-party inventory defines supply-chain, privacy, CSP, postMessage, OAuth, payment, and unsafe-consumption test boundaries.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Application Architecture

items.remediation: Maintain an approved dependency inventory, minimize shared data and browser privilege, pin/integrity-protect suitable assets, and remove unused integrations.

items.title: Catalog browser storage keys and client configuration namespaces
items.objective: Identify localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, Cache Storage, and non-session cookie namespaces used by representative application flows.
steps: Record storage before interacting with the application
Repeat after login and representative features
Classify keys by purpose without retaining secret values
Map keys to scripts and requests that create or consume them

examples.note: Record a key as auth.token = [redacted, JWT-like] rather than copying the token into evidence.

items.manipulate: Normal browser workflows in a designated test profile
items.secure_behavior: Client storage use is inventoried, purpose-limited, and does not retain unnecessary sensitive data.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later test confirms sensitive data exposure or unsafe trust in editable storage; a key name alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Clear the profile and repeat to distinguish application state from extensions, stale origins, and unrelated tabs.
false_positives: Browser extensions can add storage entries
Opaque identifiers may be non-sensitive preferences rather than credentials
items.impact: Storage inventory supports token, DOM, offline cache, service worker, and client-side trust testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webpage Content for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Keep sensitive state server-side where possible, minimize browser retention, and never trust editable client storage for authorization decisions.

items.title: Identify upload, download, import, and export entry points
items.objective: Catalog every route that accepts, generates, transforms, previews, imports, or returns user-influenced files.
steps: Trace UI controls and API calls for upload, attachment, avatar, import, export, and preview functions
Record methods, multipart fields, media types, limits, identifiers, and storage origins
Map asynchronous processing and download routes
Note role and tenant context for later file-specific tests

examples.request:
POST /api/attachments HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=BOUNDARY
examples.note: Use an inert text canary during mapping.

items.manipulate: Normal inert file operations on disposable test records
items.secure_behavior: All file entry points are inventoried and consistently apply documented type, size, storage, authorization, and lifecycle controls.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later file-handling test confirms execution, traversal, unauthorized access, or unsafe processing; discovery alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Correlate UI, request, processing status, and retrieval route; distinguish direct application handling from third-party storage widgets.
false_positives: A file picker can upload directly to an out-of-scope provider
Export buttons can generate reports without accepting user files
items.impact: Complete file-flow inventory is required for upload, download, inclusion, archive, parser, and authorization coverage.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Maintain one file-flow inventory and apply centralized validation, isolated storage/processing, authorization, quotas, and cleanup controls.
items.safety: Use inert, small canary files and disposable records; do not upload active content or trigger heavy document processing during discovery.

items.title: Map search, filtering, sorting, and reporting inputs
items.objective: Inventory query-building features and their structured inputs before injection, authorization, and resource-abuse testing.
prerequisites: Representative searchable data in a test account
steps: Exercise search, filters, sorting, pagination, saved views, and reports normally
Record parameter names, operators, encodings, and defaults
Identify free text versus structured expression inputs
Map export or asynchronous report-generation paths
items.manipulate: Normal search terms and filter controls using non-sensitive test data
items.secure_behavior: Search inputs and supported operators are documented and consistently constrained by authorization and resource budgets.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later test confirms interpreter injection, cross-user data access, or disproportionate resource use; flexible search alone is not a finding.
items.validation: Correlate each control to request syntax and response behavior; do not assume backend technology from operator names.
false_positives: Client-only filtering can resemble server query parameters
Search syntax may be intentionally expressive but safely parsed and authorized
items.impact: Search inventory focuses injection, BOLA, excessive-data, pagination, and rate-abuse testing.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Identify Application Entry Points

items.remediation: Define explicit query grammars, parameterize backend operations, enforce object authorization, and bound result size and computational cost.

items.title: Record error-response families without forcing exceptional load
items.objective: Classify validation, authentication, authorization, missing-route, and server error responses to guide later differential testing.
prerequisites: Harmless malformed values and missing paths
steps: Capture normal success responses
Trigger one harmless validation error and one unique missing path
Record status, media type, body schema, correlation ID, and cache behavior
Use naturally observed server errors rather than attempting to crash the service
items.manipulate: A unique missing path and one type-safe invalid value
items.secure_behavior: Errors are consistent, minimally informative, traceable for operators, and do not reveal secrets or internal stack details.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An error discloses valid secrets or sensitive internals with demonstrated utility, or creates a differential that later confirms a security weakness.
items.validation: Repeat against a control and distinguish application errors from proxy, CDN, WAF, and browser-generated pages.
false_positives: Correlation IDs and generic error codes are usually operationally useful
A product-like error page can be generated by an upstream proxy
items.impact: Error families support reliable false-positive analysis and can reveal sensitive implementation detail when disclosure is substantive.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Review Webpage Content for Information Leakage

items.remediation: Return generic client errors, log detailed diagnostics only in protected systems, avoid secret-bearing exceptions, and preserve safe correlation identifiers.

items.title: Establish role, tenant, and account test matrices from observed functionality
items.objective: Create a coverage matrix linking available test identities to roles, tenants, ownership states, and reachable functions before authorization testing.
prerequisites: Known roles or a plan to discover them
steps: Record each designated account's role, tenant, groups, and lifecycle state
Browse the same top-level functions with each identity
List objects owned, shared, and unowned by each account
Identify missing comparison accounts and mark blocked authorization work

examples.note: Matrix columns can be tenant A member, tenant A admin, tenant B member, and unauthenticated; never include credentials in the sheet.

items.manipulate: Normal navigation using designated test identities
items.secure_behavior: Test coverage can represent every important authorization boundary without using production-user accounts.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A later comparison confirms unauthorized function or object access; menu differences or role names alone are not findings.
items.validation: Confirm role and tenant attributes from owner records or safe account UI, and verify that each account is designated for testing.
false_positives: Hidden menus can coexist with correct server authorization
Role labels can differ while effective permissions are identical
items.impact: A complete matrix is necessary to detect horizontal, vertical, object, field, and cross-tenant authorization failures.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Execution Paths Through Application

items.remediation: Provision dedicated least-privilege comparison accounts for assessments and maintain an authoritative role/tenant permission model.

items.title: Create the confirmed in-scope attack-surface register
items.objective: Consolidate approved assets, applications, operations, identities, data flows, dependencies, confidence, ownership, and test constraints into one traceable register.
prerequisites: Completed initial passive and active reconnaissance
Owner available to resolve scope questions
steps: Merge hostname, application, route, API, identity, file, channel, and dependency inventories
Assign owner, environment, data sensitivity, and confidence
Separate confirmed in-scope, dependency-only, pending, and excluded entries
Record safe-test limits and link every later methodology item to applicable surfaces

examples.note: A useful entry records asset, application, environment, owner, evidence, scope state, confidence, data class, and test constraints.

items.manipulate: Inventory records only; no additional target interaction
items.secure_behavior: Every tested surface has explicit scope, ownership, data handling, and safety context, with uncertainty visibly tracked.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A material live surface remains unowned or outside the agreed assessment plan after owner confirmation; the register itself does not create a vulnerability.
items.validation: Review the register with the owner and reconcile each pending item before active tests; preserve evidence for every inclusion decision.
false_positives: Duplicate DNS names can represent one application
A third-party dependency can be relevant to architecture without being authorized for testing
items.impact: The register controls coverage, prevents unauthorized activity, and provides the basis for context-aware applicability and reporting.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Map Application Architecture

items.remediation: Assign durable ownership, lifecycle, data classification, and assessment constraints to every application asset and update the register as architecture changes.

items.title: Identify dangling DNS records that enable subdomain takeover
items.objective: Determine whether in-scope hostnames resolve to expired, unclaimed, or deprovisioned third-party resources that an attacker could claim, without ever claiming them during testing.
prerequisites: Written authorization for DNS and third-party service reconnaissance of in-scope hostnames
The hostname inventory assembled in earlier enumeration steps
steps: Resolve each in-scope hostname and record A, CNAME, NS, and alias targets together with the responsible provider
Look for NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, unclaimed provider endpoints, and deprovisioned-service responses
Identify the provider claim model (pages, storage, app platforms) and whether the target is currently claimed
Document the record class, provider, and evidence, then stop before any registration, claim, or content upload
Deliver an identification report with per-record remediation instead of demonstrating a takeover

examples.note: Evidence is limited to DNS responses and provider claim-state indicators; no third-party resource is registered or modified.

items.manipulate: One hostname and one record class at a time
items.secure_behavior: DNS records reference only active, owner-verified third-party resources, and deprovisioning removes or re-verifies every record.
items.vulnerable_behavior: a record resolves to a resource that is unclaimed or expired and could be taken over under the provider's claim model
items.validation: Pair the DNS resolution with provider-specific unclaimed indicators such as claimable error pages or deprovisioned endpoints; a DNS failure alone is insufficient.
false_positives: service-provider responses can look unclaimed during migrations
wildcard DNS or parked pages can mimic deprovisioned endpoints
items.impact: A takeable record lets an attacker host content on the victim subdomain after claiming it, enabling phishing, cookie capture, and origin-confusion abuse.
evidence: DNS resolution output for each affected hostname
Provider responses showing the unclaimed or expired state
Claim-model documentation and the remediation note per record

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Test for Subdomain Takeover

items.safety: Identification and reporting only. Never register, claim, point, or upload to the dangling resource; taking over the hostname changes third-party state and is outside the scope of an authorized assessment.
items.remediation: Remove or re-point dangling records, verify ownership of every third-party resource referenced by DNS, and add deprovisioning checks to offboarding.
do_not_report: Do not report every unclaimed record as critical; weight the record class (NS over CNAME), the provider claim model, and the hostname's criticality, and deliver remediation guidance rather than a claimed takeover.
